title-group.article-title: Drug A against placebo in older patients with high blood pressure

sec.title: Background
sec.p: High blood pressure raises the risk of stroke.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We randomised 400 adults to drug A or placebo for twelve months.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Systolic pressure fell more with drug A than with placebo.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Drug A lowered blood pressure in this trial.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: High blood pressure is common in older adults 1, and it is a leading cause of stroke [2–3]. Many patients need more than one drug to reach their target 4. Treatment lowered the stroke rate in older patients.

We asked whether a new drug could lower pressure safely over one year, and whether the effect differed by age. The question matters because current options often fail to bring pressure under control in this group.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Adults aged 60 years or more with untreated high blood pressure were invited from twelve clinics. Each person was assigned by a computer list to drug A or to placebo, and nobody knew which was given. Blood pressure was measured at the clinic every three months by trained nurses using the same device.

caption.p: Flow of patients through the trial.

sec.p: The main outcome was the change in systolic pressure at twelve months. We compared groups with a simple t test and counted adverse events in each group.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: In total 400 patients took part, and 372 finished the study. Table 1 gives the starting values in each group, which were close.

Systolic pressure fell by 14 mmHg with drug A and by 6 mmHg with placebo. Results by outcome are in Table 2.Table 2Outcomes at twelve months

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Drug A lowered pressure more than placebo, which agrees with earlier small studies. The trial was short, and longer follow up is needed to show an effect on stroke itself.
